library(rstudioapi)
library(ggcorrplot)
library(corrr)
library(data.table)
library(lmtest)
library(MASS)
library(tree)
library(vip)
library(car)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)

# This is the project path
setwd("E:/TB1/Urban Analytics and City Science/Seoul-Bike-Data-Analysis-main")

# Load data
bike_data = read.csv("SeoulBikeData.csv",
                     header = TRUE,
                     sep = ",",
                     quote = "\"",
                     comment.char = "",
                     stringsAsFactors = TRUE,
                     check.names = F)
# Change column names
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Rented Bike Count")] <- "RentedBikeCount"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Temperature")] <- "Temperature"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Humidity(%)")] <- "Humidity"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Wind speed (m/s)")] <- "WindSpeed"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Visibility (10m)")] <- "Visibility"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Dew point temperature")] <- "DewPointTemp"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Solar Radiation (MJ/m2)")] <- "SolarRad"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Rainfall(mm)")] <- "Rainfall"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Snowfall (cm)")] <- "Snowfall"
colnames(bike_data)[which(names(bike_data) == "Functioning Day")] <- "FunctioningDay"

View(bike_data)

# Check for Null Values
sum(is.na(bike_data))
## [1] 0
# Split data into train and test
set.seed(20)
n = nrow(bike_data)
idx_tr <- sample(n,round(0.8*n),replace=FALSE)
# Removing the date column from test and train data
train <- bike_data[idx_tr,-1]
test <- bike_data[-idx_tr,-1]

train_copy = copy(train)
# Correlation Matrix of y with numeric predictors
bike.subset <- subset(bike_data, select = c(RentedBikeCount, Hour, Temperature, Humidity, WindSpeed, 
                                            Visibility, DewPointTemp, SolarRad,Snowfall,Rainfall))

pairs(~., data = bike.subset, main = "Scatterplot Matrix")

# Correlation Heatmap
library(corrplot)
library(RColorBrewer)
CR <-cor(train[,c(-11,-12,-13)])
corrplot(CR, type="lowe", order="hclust",
         col=brewer.pal(n=8, name="RdYlBu"), main = "Correlation Heatmap")

View(CR)
# Normalise data to create boxplots of variables
train_copy$Hour<-scale(train_copy$Hour)
train_copy$Temperature<-scale(train_copy$Temperature)
train_copy$Humidity<-scale(train_copy$Humidity)
train_copy$WindSpeed<-scale(train_copy$WindSpeed)
train_copy$Visibility<-scale(train_copy$Visibility)
train_copy$DewPointTemp<-scale(train_copy$DewPointTemp)
train_copy$SolarRad<-scale(train_copy$SolarRad)
train_copy$Rainfall<-scale(train_copy$Rainfall)
train_copy$Snowfall<-scale(train_copy$Snowfall)

norm_num = subset(train_copy, select = c(Hour, Temperature, Humidity, WindSpeed, 
                                              Visibility, DewPointTemp, SolarRad,Snowfall, Rainfall))
# Boxplot
boxplot(norm_num, xlab="Normalised Variables", main = "Boxplot of Numeric Predictors")

# Create a full model
full_model = lm(RentedBikeCount ~ ., data = train)
summary(full_model)

# Check for influential points
count_influential = sum(cooks.distance(full_model) > 4 / nrow(train))
count_influential
## [1] 292
# Outliers in Train data
out_ind <- which(abs(rstandard(full_model))>2)
count_out <- sum(abs(rstandard(full_model))>2)
count_out
## [1] 361
# No invalid outliers. Do not delete

# In the summary output of the full model, visibility has a high p-value
# It might not be significant
# Check if visibility is significant using anova

# H0 : Beta for Visibility is 0
# H1 : Beta for Visibility is not 0

full_noVis = lm(RentedBikeCount ~ .-Visibility, data = train)
summary(full_noVis)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RentedBikeCount ~ . - Visibility, data = train)

anova(full_model,full_noVis)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Model 1: RentedBikeCount ~ Hour + Temperature + Humidity + WindSpeed + 
##     Visibility + DewPointTemp + SolarRad + Rainfall + Snowfall + 
##     Seasons + Holiday + FunctioningDay
## Model 2: RentedBikeCount ~ (Hour + Temperature + Humidity + WindSpeed + 
##     Visibility + DewPointTemp + SolarRad + Rainfall + Snowfall + 
##     Seasons + Holiday + FunctioningDay) - Visibility
##   Res.Df        RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
## 1   6993 1303594421                           
## 2   6994 1303774155 -1   -179733 0.9642 0.3262
# p-value for Visibility (0.971) is greater than 0.05
# Do not reject H0 and conclude that visibilty is  not important
# Rather than manualy picking variables, we decided to use selection procedures in R to pick the most important variables

# Perform variable selection using forward, backward, stepwise methods using AIC and BIC as the criterion to compare

# Model 1 : Forward selection - AIC
null_model = lm(RentedBikeCount ~ 1, data = train)
for_model_aic = step(null_model, scope = RentedBikeCount ~ Hour + Temperature + Humidity + 
                   WindSpeed + Visibility + DewPointTemp + SolarRad + Rainfall + Snowfall + 
                   Seasons + Holiday + FunctioningDay, direction = "forward", trace = 0)
summary(for_model_aic)

# Model 2 : Forward selection - BIC
n = nrow(train)
for_model_bic = step(null_model, scope = RentedBikeCount ~ Hour + Temperature + Humidity + 
                       WindSpeed + Visibility + DewPointTemp + SolarRad + Rainfall + Snowfall + 
                       Seasons + Holiday + FunctioningDay, direction = "forward", trace = 0, k = log(n))
summary(for_model_bic)

summary(back_model_aic)

# Model 5 : Stepwise Selection - AIC
null_model = lm(RentedBikeCount ~ 1, data = train)
step_aic = step(null_model, scope = RentedBikeCount ~ Hour + Temperature + Humidity + 
                  WindSpeed + Visibility + DewPointTemp + SolarRad + Rainfall + Snowfall + 
                  Seasons + Holiday + FunctioningDay, direction = "both", trace = 0)
summary(step_aic)

# Model 6 : Stepwise Selection - BIC
n = nrow(train)
step_bic = step(full_model, direction = "both", trace = 0, k = log(n))
summary(step_bic)

# We see that Temperature and DewPointTemp are highly correlated. Let'se try to drop Dew and check its significance
base_model_NoDew = lm(RentedBikeCount ~ Temperature + Hour + FunctioningDay + Humidity + 
                        Seasons + Rainfall + SolarRad + Holiday + 
                        Snowfall + WindSpeed, data = train)

anova(base_model, base_model_NoDew)
## Analysis of Variance Table

# p-value is very low (0.001214)
# DewPointTemp is significant, even though it is corr with Temperature

# Try to drop Temperature and compare
base_model_NoTemp = lm(RentedBikeCount ~ DewPointTemp + Hour + FunctioningDay + Humidity + 
                        Seasons + Rainfall + SolarRad + Holiday +

# Try Boxcox on this model
eps = 1e-2
n = nrow(train)

model_eps = lm((RentedBikeCount + mu) ~ Temperature + Hour + FunctioningDay + Humidity + 
                 Seasons + Rainfall + SolarRad + Holiday + 
                 Snowfall+ DewPointTemp + WindSpeed, data = train)

lambda = 0.75

                  Seasons + Rainfall + SolarRad + Holiday + 
                  Snowfall+ DewPointTemp + WindSpeed, data = train)
summary(box_model)

     main = "Model Residuals v/s Fitted Vales")
abline(h = 0, col = 'red')

# 2. Equal Variance  - Violated

##  studentized Breusch-Pagan test
## 
## data:  model_ThreeWay_NoVIF
## BP = 684.19, df = 13, p-value < 2.2e-16
# p-value is 2.2e-16

# 3. Normality - Violated
qqnorm(resid(model_ThreeWay_NoVIF), main = "Normal Q-Q Plot", col = "darkgrey")
qqline(resid(model_ThreeWay_NoVIF), col = "dodgerblue", lwd = 2)

residuals <-resid(model_ThreeWay_NoVIF)
shapiro.test(residuals[0:5000])

##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
##

# p-value = 2.2e-16

# Try Boxcox Transformation on model_ThreeWay_NoVIF

eps = 1e-2
n = nrow(train)

model_eps = lm((RentedBikeCount + mu )~ Temperature + Hour + FunctioningDay + Humidity 
               + Rainfall + SolarRad + Holiday + 
                 Visibility:Hour + Seasons:WindSpeed 
               + Temperature:Humidity:SolarRad, data = train)
boxcox(model_eps)

boxcox(model_eps, lambda = seq(0.5, 1.0, by = 0.05))

lambda = 0.75
box_model <- lm((((RentedBikeCount + mu)^(lambda)-1)/(lambda)) ~ Temperature + Hour + FunctioningDay + Humidity 
                + Rainfall + SolarRad + Holiday + 
                  Visibility:Hour + Seasons:WindSpeed 
                + Temperature:Humidity:SolarRad, data = train)
summary(box_model)

# Check assumptions

model_transform1_noVIF = lm(RentedBikeCount ~ I(Temperature^3) + Hour + FunctioningDay + 
                              Humidity  + I(exp(-Rainfall)) + 
                              SolarRad + Holiday + Temperature:Humidity + 
                              Visibility:Hour + Seasons:WindSpeed + SolarRad:Temperature + 
                              Temperature:Humidity:SolarRad, data = train)

basline = model_transform1_noVIF
model_interacPoly = model_transform1_noVIF

# 1. Linearity - Violated
plot(fitted.values(basline), residuals(basline), xlab = "Fitted Values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Model Residuals v/s Fitted Vales")
abline(h = 0, col = 'red')

# 2. Equal Variance  - Violated
bptest(basline)
## 
##  studentized Breusch-Pagan test
## 
## data:  basline
## BP = 676.68, df = 15, p-value < 2.2e-16
# p-value is 2.2e-16

# 3. Normality - Violated
qqnorm(resid(basline), main = "Normal Q-Q Plot", col = "darkgrey")
qqline(resid(basline), col = "dodgerblue", lwd = 2)

residuals <-resid(basline)
shapiro.test(residuals[0:5000])
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  residuals[0:5000]
## W = 0.94598, p-value < 2.2e-16
# Boxcox Transformation
eps = 1e-2
n = nrow(train)
mu = seq(min(train$RentedBikeCount) + eps, max(train$RentedBikeCount), length = n)

model_eps = lm((RentedBikeCount + mu) ~ I(Temperature^3) + Hour + FunctioningDay + 
                 Humidity  + I(exp(-Rainfall)) + 
                 SolarRad + Holiday + Temperature:Humidity + 
                 Visibility:Hour + Seasons:WindSpeed + SolarRad:Temperature + 
                 Temperature:Humidity:SolarRad, data = train)
boxcox(model_eps)

boxcox(model_eps, lambda = seq(0.5, 1.0, by = 0.05))

lambda = 0.75
box_model_final <- lm((((RentedBikeCount + mu)^(lambda)-1)/(lambda)) ~ I(Temperature^3) + Hour + FunctioningDay + 
                        Humidity  + I(exp(-Rainfall)) + 
                        SolarRad + Holiday + Temperature:Humidity + 
                        Visibility:Hour + Seasons:WindSpeed + SolarRad:Temperature + 
                        Temperature:Humidity:SolarRad, data = train)
summary(box_model_final)

## [1] 0.5422511
# R2: chooses model_interactions
summary(model_before_interac)$r.squared
## [1] 0.5501867
summary(model_interactions)$r.squared
## [1] 0.5557024
summary(model_interacPoly)$r.squared
## [1] 0.543231
n = nrow(train)
# RMSE - train
# Chooses model_interactions
sqrt(sum(resid(model_before_interac)^2)/n)
## [1] 431.3245
sqrt(sum(resid(model_interactions)^2)/n)
## [1] 428.6719
sqrt(sum(resid(model_interacPoly)^2)/n)
## [1] 434.6466
# RMSE - test
rmse = function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted) ^ 2))
}

# chooses model_interactions
rmse(predict(model_before_interac, newdata = test), test$RentedBikeCount)
## [1] 437.9837
rmse(predict(model_interactions, newdata = test), test$RentedBikeCount)
## [1] 439.5629
rmse(predict(model_interacPoly, newdata = test), test$RentedBikeCount)
## [1] 444.1792
# PRESS (or RMSE with LOOCV)
# Chooses model_interactions
sqrt(sum((resid(model_before_interac)/(1-hatvalues(model_before_interac)))^2)/n)
## [1] 432.2446
sqrt(sum((resid(model_interactions)/(1-hatvalues(model_interactions)))^2)/n)
## [1] 429.5843
sqrt(sum((resid(model_interacPoly)/(1-hatvalues(model_interacPoly)))^2)/n)
## [1] 435.6208
# BEST PERFORMING MODEL IS MODEL_INTERACTIONS

# Lets try to use log transformation on it to see if it meets assumptions
# Try to fix it by transforming both y and x

# Response Transformation
model_log = lm(log(RentedBikeCount + 1) ~ Temperature + Hour + 
                 FunctioningDay + Humidity + Rainfall + SolarRad + 
                 Holiday + Visibility:Hour + Seasons:WindSpeed + 
                  Temperature:Humidity:SolarRad, data = train)
summary(model_log)

# 1. Lasso 
library(glmnet)
xtrain = model.matrix(RentedBikeCount~.,train)[,-1]
ytrain = train[,1]

xtest = model.matrix(RentedBikeCount~.,test)[,-1]
ytest = test[,1]


fit_lasso_cv = cv.glmnet(xtrain, ytrain, alpha = 1, trace = 0)
plot(fit_lasso_cv)

bestlam = fit_lasso_cv$lambda.min;bestlam
## [1] 0.3535835
fit_lasso_best = glmnet(xtrain, ytrain, alpha = 1, lambda = bestlam)
coef(fit_lasso_best)

actual <- train$RentedBikeCount

rss <- sum((preds - actual) ^ 2)

rsq <- 1 - rss/tss
rsq
## [1] 0.5502021
# Check model assumptions for Lasso model with best lambda

# 1. Equal Variance  - Violated
bptest(basline)
## 
##  studentized Breusch-Pagan test
## 
## data:  basline
## BP = 676.68, df = 15, p-value < 2.2e-16
# p-value is 2.2e-16

# 2. Normality - Violated
qqnorm(resid(basline), main = "Normal Q-Q Plot", col = "darkgrey")
qqline(resid(basline), col = "dodgerblue", lwd = 2)

residuals <-resid(basline)
shapiro.test(residuals[0:5000])
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  residuals[0:5000]
## W = 0.94598, p-value < 2.2e-16
# 3. Ridge
fit_ridge_cv = cv.glmnet(xtrain, ytrain, alpha = 0, trace = 0)
plot(fit_ridge_cv)

bestlam = fit_ridge_cv$lambda.min;bestlam
## [1] 34.54546
fit_ridge_best = glmnet(xtrain, ytrain, alpha = 0, lambda = bestlam)
coef(fit_ridge_best)

Analysis Report: Demand Forecast for Bike Sharing Rental in Seoul

Abstract

### This report explores the Seoul shared bicycle dataset with the aim of forecasting the rental demand for shared bicycles by forecasting the rental demand for shared bicycles. Through exploratory data analysis (EDA), regression models and decision tree models, this study analyses the key factors that affect rental demand, and evaluates the performance of the models. The pruned regression tree demonstrats good prediction accuracy and shows good results.

1.Introduction With the growing urban population, shared bikes have become a sustainable and efficient mode of transport. Accurately predicting the rental demand for shared bikes is crucial for optimising the supply of bikes and improving users’ satisfaction. This study analyses the shared bicycle dataset in Seoul to understand how factors such as weather and time affect rental demand. Through regression models and decision tree models, this study seeks to make a balance between prediction accuracy and model simplicity. —

2. Data overview This dataset contains hour-by-hour records of Seoul’s bike-sharing system with the target variable RentedBikeCount (number of rented bikes). The key predictor variables include weather conditions (e.g., temperature, humidity, wind speed), time variables (e.g., hours, seasons), and categorical variables (e.g., holidays, weekdays). The dataset contains 8760 records with the following attributes: Target variable: RentedBikeCount (number of rentals per hour) Predictor variables: Numeric: temperature, humidity, wind speed, visibility, solar radiation, rainfall, snowfall Categorical variables: season, holiday, weekday Time variables: hourly

Data preprocessing The following steps were performed in the initial pre-processing: standardisation of column name formats; removing irrelevant Date columns; processing outliers while retaining realistic extreme values. —

3. Exploratory data analysis (EDA) EDA reveals trends and relationships between variables. Scatter plots show weak correlations between RentedBikeCount and some of the predictor variables (e.g., rainfall), while hourly demand shows a clear cycling pattern. The correlation heatmap highlights strong correlations between temperature and dew point temperature, which can exclude DewPointTemp. Key Findings: 1. demand for cycle hire peaks in the morning and evening peak hours; 2. weather has a significant impact on demand, with temperature and humidity being strong predictors; 3. rental volumes are lower on holidays, largely due to reduced commuting. —

4. Methodology In this study, linear regression and decision tree methods are used to model RentedBikeCount, and the dataset is divided into training and test sets in 80-20 ratio. The model performance is evaluated by RMSE and R-squared metrics. —

4.1 Linear regression The full regression model includes all predictor variables: lm_full <- lm(RentedBikeCount ~ ., data = train) Despite that the R-squared value is ajusted into 0.55, residual analyses shows that the assumption of linearity is violated. A simplified model with close performance is obtained by a step-by-step feature selection. —

4.2 Decision Tree Models The regression tree is trained using the tree package: unpruned_tree <- tree(RentedBikeCount ~ ., data = train) Key features of the unpruned tree: Terminal nodes: 13 Predictor variables used: temperature, season, hour, humidity, solar radiation, weekday, rainfall Mean deviation of residuals: 122,000 —

4.3 Decision Tree Pruning and Cross Validation The ideal tree size of 8 terminal nodes has been determined through a cross-validation. The pruning operation reduces the complexity of the model and makes it more stable on new data: pruned_tree_8 <- prune.tree(unpruned_tree, best = 8) The pruned tree behaves as follows: training RMSE: 389 test RMSE: 395 —

4.4 Advanced modelling and feature engineering In order to get better relationships between variables and to solve the problem of strong correlations between variables, subsequent models incorporate two-by-two and three-by-three interaction terms, including: Two-by-two interactions: temperature × humidity, visibility × hours, season × wind speed Three-way interactions: temperature × solar radiation × humidity Although the inclusion of the interaction terms results in a slight improvement in the R² value (to 0.5823), there are still strong correlations between some of the key variables (higher VIF). By gradually optimising the model (e.g. removing variables with high VIF), the model becomes more stable and the VIF is within a reasonable range, but the R² value decreases to around 0.5557. —

5. Results and discussion 5.1 Model performance | Model | Adjusted R-squared | Training RMSE | Test RMSE | | ——– | —–: | :—-: | :—-: | | Full regression model | 0.547 | 433 | 429 | | Pruned decision tree | N/A | 389 | 395 | | Interaction Model | 0.550 | 432 | 425 | | Polynomial Model | 0.538 | 437 | 432 | Decision trees perform better in RMSE than regression models, especially on training data. This is due to the fact that it can handle complex non-linear relationships better, but its results are less easy to interpret compared to the regression model.

5.2 Importance of variables The decision tree shows that Temperature, Hour and Seasons are the most important predictor variables. In particular, weather-related variables have the greatest impact on demand fluctuations. —

6. Conclusion This study successfully develops a forecasting model for hour-by-hour rental demand of shared bikes in Seoul, testing the effectiveness of regression models and decision trees. The advantage of the regression model is that the results are easy to understand, but the decision tree performs better in terms of accuracy of prediction. Future research could try to use more advanced methods, such as random forests or gradient boosting trees, to further improve the predictive effectiveness of the model. —

References 1)Sathishkumar V E & Yongyun Cho (2020) A rule-based model for Seoul Bike sharing demand prediction using weather data, European Journal of Remote Sensing, 53:sup1, 166-183, DOI: 10.1080/22797254.2020.1725789 2)Aditya Singh Kashyap & Swastika Swastik (2021), “Regression Model to Predict Bike Sharing Demand”, International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology, Volume 6 Issue 3, ISSN No:2456-2165 3)https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Seoul+Bike+Sharing+Demand
